tagline: An old turnpike’s switchbacks climb to the earthworks of Cheat Summit Fort
intro: Cheat Mountain Backway follows a short section of the original Staunton-Parkersburg Turnpike south of U.S. 250, switchbacking up Cheat Mountain. The Federal Highway Administration gives the backway’s length as 3.32 miles and allows 15 minutes for the drive. Its destination is Cheat Summit Fort, a Monongahela National Forest site with interpretive trails and an overlook. White Top stands west of Shavers Fork and Cheat Bridge; the original turnpike crossed the knob, while U.S. 250 now skirts its base.

General George B. McClellan ordered the fort built in 1861 to secure the turnpike and protect the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad. Construction began on July 16 on White Top, a 4,085-foot knob. The fort guarded the turnpike where it crossed about 100 feet below. Severe weather and strategic changes led to its abandonment in April 1862. Snow was reported on August 13 in the camp’s first year, and horses froze to death in mid-September.

Begin near Cheat Bridge, where U.S. 250 crosses Shavers Fork. The old turnpike climbs toward the summit fort; modern U.S. 250 skirts White Top’s base beside the river. Beyond the fort, the turnpike is impassable, so the backway returns to the highway on the more direct, signed Cheat Summit Fort road.
notice: The fort’s earthworks remain at the summit.

moments.title: Cheat Bridge
moments.text: Cheat Bridge has carried more than one generation of road across Shavers Fork. A covered bridge served the Staunton-Parkersburg Turnpike before the Civil War. Returning more than 40 years after his wartime service, Ambrose Bierce described soldiers’ names carved into its wood. The bridge on the old turnpike alignment is now a steel truss built in 1912 by the Canton Bridge Company. U.S. 250 moved downstream in 1934; that crossing’s original steel bridge was replaced in 2021. The 1912 bridge carries County Route 250/4, distinct from the highway’s newer crossing.

moments.title: Cheat Summit Fort
moments.text: Earthworks survive from the Union camp that guarded the turnpike from White Top. Construction began in July 1861, and the fort remained occupied until April 1862. In September, Confederate forces failed to capture it. From its position above the turnpike, Fort Milroy helped guard the entrance to the Tygart Valley River valley to the west. Weather and success in driving Confederate forces from the area contributed to the decision to abandon the fort. Interpretive trails and an overlook now explain the site. Cheat Summit was the highest Union camp of the Civil War.
moments.notice: The encampment’s surviving earthworks mark the fortified summit.

moments.title: Fort Milroy Cemetery
moments.text: South of the fort, depressions in the ground mark emptied graves. The cemetery held people who died at Fort Milroy, but all the bodies were exhumed after the Civil War. Many were reinterred at West Virginia National Cemetery in Grafton. The visible hollows are the traces of those former burials.
moments.notice: Depressions from the emptied graves remain visible.

practical: Cheat Summit Fort: The turnpike beyond the fort is impassable. Return to U.S. 250 by the signed Cheat Summit Fort road. Snow sometimes closes the road. (checked 2026-10-11)
